markers.label: Vilnius
markers.description: Vilnius was claimed by Lithuania as its historic capital and by Poland as a city with deep Polish political and cultural ties.

markers.label: Kaunas
markers.description: Kaunas became Lithuania's seat of government while Vilnius remained contested.

slides.title: Allies Against Bolshevism, Rivals Over Vilnius
slides.cap: Lithuanian soldiers in Vilnius during the contested independence period.
slides.body: Poland and Lithuania both emerged from the collapse of empires with urgent security problems and incompatible national projects. Vilnius was the heart of the dispute. The city was Lithuanian in state symbolism, heavily Polish and Jewish in urban demography, and strategically important to Polish plans for a federation in the east.

stats.lbl: Border-making after empire turns partners into rivals

title: Polish Capture of Vilnius
sub: Polish forces take the disputed city

markers.label: Vilnius
markers.description: Polish forces captured Vilnius from Bolshevik control, but Lithuania saw the move as occupation of its capital.

slides.title: Liberation for One Side, Occupation for the Other
slides.cap: Visual reference for Polish Capture of Vilnius.
slides.body: Polish forces captured Vilnius in April 1919 during the Polish-Soviet War. For Warsaw, the operation removed Bolshevik control and strengthened Poland's eastern position. For Lithuania, it meant the loss of the capital to another claimant. The same battle therefore had opposite meanings from the start.

stats.lbl: The city question hardens into interstate conflict

markers.label: Sejny
markers.description: Polish forces and local fighters took Sejny from Lithuanian control during the border struggle.

markers.label: Suwałki
markers.description: The Suwałki region became a second flashpoint beyond Vilnius.

slides.title: A Local Border War
slides.body: The Sejny uprising showed that the conflict was not only about Vilnius. Around Suwałki and Sejny, mixed populations, rival administrations, and shifting demarcation lines turned local control into armed confrontation. The violence made compromise harder by tying national claims to village-level fear and revenge.

title: Foch Line and Entente Mediation
sub: Great-power lines fail to settle the border

markers.label: Suwałki region
markers.description: Entente demarcation efforts tried to separate Polish and Lithuanian forces but did not resolve sovereignty.

markers.label: Paris Peace Conference
markers.description: Western diplomats drew lines, but local armies and governments contested them.

slides.title: Lines on Paper, Forces on the Ground
slides.body: The Entente-backed Foch Line tried to reduce fighting by separating Polish and Lithuanian forces. It did not solve the deeper dispute. Both governments believed outside mediation misunderstood their security and historical claims, while armed units on the ground kept changing facts faster than diplomats could stabilize them.

stats.lbl: Diplomacy cannot keep pace with contested front lines

title: Polish-Soviet War Overlap
sub: Lithuania and Soviet Russia sign a treaty

markers.label: Moscow
markers.description: The Soviet-Lithuanian treaty recognized Lithuanian claims while the Red Army was fighting Poland.

markers.label: Vilnius
markers.description: Soviet transfer and Lithuanian entry into Vilnius occurred during Poland's crisis against the Red Army.

slides.title: The Wider War Changes the Dispute
slides.body: The Polish-Soviet War transformed the Polish-Lithuanian conflict. Soviet Russia recognized Lithuania and its claim to Vilnius in July 1920 while the Red Army advanced against Poland. Lithuania regained the city briefly, but the sequence tied Vilnius to Poland's existential war with the Soviets and made Polish leaders even less willing to accept Lithuanian control.

stats.lbl: A bilateral border dispute is pulled into the Polish-Soviet War

title: Suwałki Agreement
sub: A ceasefire that leaves Vilnius exposed

markers.label: Suwałki
markers.description: The agreement tried to halt fighting along the Suwałki line.

markers.label: Vilnius
markers.description: The agreement did not fully secure Vilnius, leaving room for the next crisis.

slides.title: A Ceasefire With a Trapdoor
slides.cap: Lithuanian and Polish delegations negotiating the Suwałki Agreement.
slides.body: The Suwałki Agreement attempted to stop Polish-Lithuanian fighting and set a demarcation line. It briefly offered diplomatic relief, but the Vilnius question remained exposed. Within days, a Polish-aligned force under Lucjan Żeligowski moved on the city, turning the agreement into a symbol of failed mediation for Lithuania.

stats.lbl: Ceasefire fails to protect Vilnius from the next move

markers.label: Vilnius
markers.description: Żeligowski's force captured the city and created a Polish-backed fait accompli.

markers.label: Vilnius approaches
markers.description: The operation was framed as a mutiny, but Lithuania viewed it as Polish aggression.

slides.title: A Plausibly Deniable Seizure
slides.cap: Lithuanian soldiers fighting Żeligowski's forces near Vievis.
slides.body: General Lucjan Żeligowski's so-called mutiny seized Vilnius and created the Republic of Central Lithuania. The move let Poland deny direct responsibility while achieving its strategic goal. For Lithuania, it confirmed that agreements and mediation could be bypassed by force. The event poisoned relations for the entire interwar period.

stats.lbl: A military fait accompli freezes the dispute

markers.label: Vilnius
markers.description: Central Lithuania used Vilnius as the center of a Polish-aligned statelet.

markers.label: Kaunas
markers.description: Lithuania refused to accept the new entity and kept Kaunas as its temporary capital.

slides.title: Statelet as Strategy
slides.cap: Visual reference for Republic of Central Lithuania.
slides.body: The Republic of Central Lithuania functioned as a buffer and political bridge toward incorporation into Poland. It gave the seizure of Vilnius a local institutional form, but Lithuania rejected its legitimacy. The result was not a settled compromise; it was a frozen conflict dressed in state paperwork.

stats.lbl: Creates the path to Polish annexation

title: League of Nations Mediation
sub: International talks fail to repair relations

markers.label: Geneva
markers.description: League mediation attempted to find a political settlement but could not bridge the Vilnius dispute.

markers.label: Kaunas
markers.description: Lithuania maintained its claim and refused normal relations with Poland.

slides.title: No Settlement From Geneva
slides.cap: Visual reference for League of Nations Mediation.
slides.body: League of Nations mediation could not reconcile the competing claims. Proposed plebiscites, federative ideas, and demarcation schemes all ran into distrust and incompatible national narratives. The failure mattered because it left two neighboring states diplomatically frozen while the wider region remained insecure.

stats.lbl: International mediation fails to normalize Polish-Lithuanian relations

title: International and Human Dimensions
sub: Mixed communities live inside rival national projects

markers.label: Vilnius region
markers.description: Poles, Lithuanians, Jews, Belarusians, and others lived inside a city claimed by competing states.

markers.label: Suwałki-Sejny region
markers.description: Border violence made local identity and security inseparable from national politics.

slides.title: The Human Geography of a Border War
slides.cap: Visual reference for International and Human Dimensions.
slides.body: The war's human dimension was rooted in mixed communities. Vilnius was not a simple national space, and neither was the Suwałki-Sejny region. Families, schools, churches, synagogues, veterans, and local officials all found themselves inside rival state projects. That is why the dispute lasted beyond battlefield operations: it was about belonging as much as borders.

stats.lbl: Local communities absorb the cost of national border-making

title: Outcome and Legacy
sub: Vilnius enters Poland; Lithuania refuses closure

markers.label: Vilnius
markers.description: Poland incorporated Vilnius after Central Lithuania's election and annexation process.

markers.label: Kaunas
markers.description: Kaunas remained Lithuania's temporary capital and the symbol of refusal to accept the loss of Vilnius.

slides.title: A Frozen Victory
slides.cap: Visual reference for Outcome and Legacy.
slides.body: Poland gained Vilnius, but the outcome did not produce reconciliation. Lithuania treated Kaunas as a temporary capital and refused normal diplomatic relations with Poland for years. The Polish-Lithuanian War therefore ended with a winner on the map and a lasting rupture in regional politics.

stats.lbl: The dispute shapes the entire interwar relationship
